title: The Chasqui Relay Runners
text:
The Inca Empire, which in the early sixteenth century stretched along the Andes from modern Ecuador to Chile, had no horses, no wheeled vehicles and no alphabet. Yet its rulers in Cusco received news from distant provinces with remarkable speed. They did it with teams of relay runners called chasquis.

Along the great network of Inca roads stood small huts at short intervals. In each one, runners waited in shifts. When a chasqui came up the road, he called out or blew a conch shell to warn the next station. A fresh runner joined him, ran alongside while the message was repeated, took any knotted cord records, called khipu, and set off at full speed toward the next post. No single man ran more than a short stage, so each could run flat out.

The Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de Leon, who traveled in Peru in the 1540s, described the system with admiration. He wrote that messages traveled along the roads faster than they could have been carried by riders on horseback, and that the posts were maintained by the surrounding communities as part of their labor duty to the state.

The system tied together an empire of millions of people across some of the most difficult terrain on Earth. It collapsed with the Spanish conquest, but parts of the roads it ran on can still be walked today.
lesson: A relay of people, each doing a short stage at full effort, can outrun any lone hero. Design work so that handoffs are quick and no one has to carry everything.
people: Chasqui runners of the Inca Empire
source: Pedro Cieza de Leon, Chronicle of Peru, part 2 (c. 1550)
